clauses.reason: Executive Order 6876 of October 16, 1934 states: "and that previous approval of the amended portions of the Code is hereby modified to include an approval of said portions of the Code in their entirety as amended" That command is a approval of an amendment to the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry and modification of the earlier approval of the amended portions under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, and it has legal effect only through that approval: under section 3(b) the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade, and under sections 3(c) and 3(f) violations were restrainable in equity and punishable as misdemeanors. Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935, provides: "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". The resolution states no other effective date, so the command ended as a prospective operative command on June 14, 1935. No earlier end is shown (see earlier_end_check). The June 16, 1935 expiry is not an end because section 1 of the resolution replaced it with April 1, 1936. Schechter (295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization, not an end date.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 6876 (October 16, 1934) is a approval of an amendment to the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry and modification of the earlier approval of the amended portions under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. Read in full from the held American Presidency Project transcription (page record checked; identity, date and subject confirmed against the census register and the WPA 1944 list); the order's own text states no limit on the approval. Its command depends entirely on the code approval, so its first end is the repeal of the code-approval and code-enforcement provisions of Title I by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 on June 14, 1935, applying SHARED_ANALYSIS.md and its adjudication; Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization only.
Member checks: {"earlier_end_check":"The order states no period, \"until\" date, condition or provisional approval that limits the approval, and no stay or postponement to a fixed date. Held orders naming the Cotton Textile Code before this order are EO 6242-C, 6242-D, 6242-E, 6407, 6424, 6463, 6476, 6420-A and EO 6858 (September 26, 1934, which, in section 9, abolishes the Cotton Textile National Industrial Relations Board created by section XVII of the code as amended July 10, 1934, and the Board of Inquiry created by EO 6840); I read the operative paragraph of each and none cancels or supersedes the code approval. No held order after October 16, 1934 names the Cotton Textile Code. The order recites that it carries out the recommendations of the Board of Inquiry for the Cotton Textile Industry created by EO 6840 of September 5, 1934; that recital commands nothing. No held record shows this code cancelled, suspended, superseded or revoked before June 14, 1935, and none shows a modification under section 10(b) that reached this order's command. June 16, 1935 is not an end, because section 1 of S.J. Res. 113 replaced that expiry with April 1, 1936. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization, not an end date.","independent_command_check":"No appointment, delegation, direction to a government agency, report direction or other command independent of the code approval appears. The \"Approval recommended\" and signature lines command nothing.","savings_check":"Read S.J. Res. 113 section 2 and its proviso and NIRA section 5 in the packet excerpts. No held source continues this approval, a prosecution under it or any command of this order after June 14, 1935; accrued acts, liabilities and the section 5 exemption for completed action are recorded as transferred or accrued and not as continued operation.","scope_check":"One operative command: approval of \"said amendment\" and modification of the previous approval of the amended portions of the code to include them as amended. The held text does not identify or reproduce the amended provisions, so I cannot test whether EO 6858 section 9 (September 26, 1934) reached any of them; the amendment takes effect only as a term of the code, and nothing in the held record shows a later modification of the amended provisions before June 14, 1935. The reference to the Board of Inquiry recommendations is a recital."}

savings.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved code before June 14, 1935 are accrued consequences, and the section 5 exemption from the antitrust laws for action complying with an approved code taken while Title I was in effect is likewise an accrued effect for completed action. The proviso to section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 names agreements and action under them, not codes, and states no time limit; the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the section 5 exemption for past action under codes, and whatever exemption survives for past action is an accrued effect, not continued operation of this approval. Nothing in the held sources continues the approval after June 14, 1935.

source_notes.date_qualification: 1935-05-27: date the section 3 delegation was declared unconstitutional; validity characterization (void from issuance under then-prevailing doctrine), not an end date
source_notes.reason: Schechter, 295 U.S. 495, held the code provisions in question invalid on both of its grounds; recorded as a validity characterization of section 3 code approvals, not as an end date for this order. It adjudicated the Live Poultry Code provisions and cancelled or withdrew no other approving order.

source_notes.date_qualification: 1933-06-16: date the Act was approved; states the repealed legal effects of a code approval, not an end date
source_notes.reason: Sections 3(a)-(f) state the legal effects of an approved code that section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed: the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition (3(b)), district courts could restrain violations (3(c)), and violations were misdemeanors (3(f)).
